svg.title: Help desk impersonation on Teams to AD CS ESC1 and ESC8 abuse kill chain
svg.desc: Single-lane kill chain from Microsoft Security Research (2026-10-30): Teams help desk impersonation, Quick Assist session, staged portable runtime, ESC1 certificate theft for privileged accounts, DCSync plus Rclone SFTP exfiltration (case 1), and PetitPotam relay to AD CS web enrollment with PKINIT (case 2). Critical stages are certificate issuance, DCSync, exfiltration and DC certificate. Detection anchors are Quick Assist launch, runtime from KB directory, CA 4886/4887, PKINIT 4768, replication 4662 and SFTP egress from file servers.
svg.text: Teams help desk impersonation into AD CS abuse: ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths
Vendor: Microsoft Security Research (2026-10-30) | Date: 2026-11-13 | Cluster: unattributed | Day 143
WORKSTATION, ACTIVE DIRECTORY AND AD CS, OCT 2026
Teams impersonation of IT help desk from external onmicrosoft.com tenants [T1566.003]
Messages and calls from organization-themed tenants with support-style display names; no Teams flaw is exploited
Pretext: urgent fix, often combined with mail bombing; Teams shows External and Scam suspected banners
Microsoft does not attribute the activity to a named actor and gives no victim sector or country
Teams chat / call from external tenant -> user is asked to open Quick Assist
Quick Assist session approved by the user: hands-on-keyboard on the workstation [T1219]
User reads the Quick Assist connection code to the caller; the attacker then drives the desktop
Rogue use of a legitimate remote tool: no malware needed for initial access
Break point: out-of-band verification, approved remote tools only, external Teams tenant restrictions
QuickAssist.exe launch shortly after external Teams contact
Archive in Downloads unpacked to a KB-prefixed staging directory, run with a portable runtime [T1204.002 T1059.007]
Portable Python, Bun or Java (a renamed Bun exe keeps its version metadata; java launches a .java source file)
Discovery: Windows version, network config, process list; LDAPS and SMB connections to domain infrastructure
Exact archive, folder and file names are not published; the KB prefix is the only path hint
bun.exe / java.exe / javaw.exe / python from %USERPROFILE%\KB* -> 636, 445
Case 1, ESC1: enumerate AD CS, request certificates as privileged accounts [T1649]
Template lets the requester supply the subject; wave 1: 3 users, 1 workstation, certs for 3 privileged accounts
About 90 min later wave 2: 16 users, second workstation, certs for 8 more privileged accounts
Defender automatic disruption cut the identities, but one privileged account was excluded and stayed usable
CA 4886/4887 request with attacker-chosen subject -> 4768 PreAuthType 16 (PKINIT)
Case 1: DCSync within seconds, then Rclone to an external SFTP server [T1003.006 T1048.002]
Certificate logon to a domain controller then DCSync; containment during the operation limited replication
Through the excluded account: file server share copied by a renamed Rclone (SearchApp.exe), 20 transfers, 3 years of files
More than 1,000 later SMB and logon attempts were blocked; the SFTP host and data volume are not published
4662 replication GUIDs from non-DC | SearchApp.exe sftp -> internet
Case 2, ESC8: PetitPotam coercion, NTLM relay to /certsrv, DC certificate, PKINIT TGT [T1187 T1557 T1649]
EFSRPC forces a DC to authenticate to an attacker host; the NTLM auth is relayed to AD CS Web Enrollment
Certificate issued from the Domain Controller template for the DC machine account, then PKINIT gives a TGT
Defender raised ESC8 alerts; the workstation was isolated and nothing further was observed
5145 efsrpc pipe | HTTP /certsrv/ from non-enrollment host | DC cert issued
Detection anchors
Sigma 01-05, KQL k1-k3, YARA (2 generic rules), Suricata sids 9993001-9993004, PEAK H1-H3. Only 3 script hashes are published.
Break points: external Teams tenants, Quick Assist, template audit, EPA on web enrollment, CA audit, replication rights, SFTP egress.
